title: Health-care payment concern reaches trust and health-policy demand through a descriptive panel bridge
source_unit: ANES 2016-2020-2024 panel respondent in official 2024 Full Release SDA tables

observations.period: 2024 pre-election; health-care payment concern × federal-government trust
observations.method: Official UC Berkeley SDA weighted row-percentage cross-tab; row V241573, column V241229, pre-election panel weight V240107a, complex stratified-cluster Taylor-series standard errors.
observations.uncertainty: Descriptive association; health-cost concern is forward-looking and not a bill or care event. Panel selection, party identity, health, income, insurance, and prior trust remain alternative explanations.
observations.subgroup: Rows defined by concern about paying health-care expenses; columns defined by federal-government trust.
observations.counterinterpretation: The trust pattern is not monotonic, and composition or prior institutional orientation may shape both concern and trust.

observations.period: 2024 pre-election to post-election; health-care payment concern × government help paying for health insurance
observations.method: Official UC Berkeley SDA weighted row-percentage cross-tab; row V241573, column V242351, post-election panel weight V240107b, complex stratified-cluster Taylor-series standard errors.
observations.uncertainty: Temporal ordering does not identify causality. Policy preference is not remedy receipt, attribution, or direct political action; post-election missingness and panel retention remain relevant.
observations.subgroup: Rows defined by pre-election concern about paying health-care expenses; columns defined by post-election preferred change in government spending to help pay for health insurance.
observations.counterinterpretation: The modest, non-monotonic policy gradient may reflect ideology, party identity, existing insurance status, health needs, or general views about government spending.

observations.method: Official UC Berkeley SDA weighted row-percentage controlled cross-tab; row V241573, column V241229, control V241227x, pre-election panel weight V240107a, complex stratified-cluster Taylor-series standard errors.
observations.uncertainty: Controlled descriptive association; several extremely-concerned party cells are small and imprecise. Party identity is conditioned, not randomly assigned, and health-cost concern remains a forward-looking proxy.
observations.subgroup: Health-cost-concern rows within seven pre-election party-identification groups; selected strong Democrat, independent, and strong Republican contrasts reported.
observations.counterinterpretation: The large level differences by party identity and weak/non-uniform within-party gradients show that pooled concern-to-trust patterns cannot be read as a universal health-cost legitimacy mechanism.

observations.counterinterpretation: Similar directional gradients within coverage groups do not prove that health-cost concern changes trust; health, income, party identity, and prior trust may explain both.

observations.uncertainty: Temporal descriptive association; several extreme-concern party cells are small and imprecise. Party identity is conditioned, not randomized, and policy preference is not remedy receipt or direct action.

boundary: This is a same-survey descriptive ANES bridge from forward-looking health-care payment concern to trust and post-election health-policy demand. It does not join MEPS or SHED respondents and does not establish that a dated bill, care decision, institutional remedy, or health-cost episode caused trust, policy preference, vote, switching, or exit. Retrieval hashes cover the two SDA query outputs used in the memo.
